planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting the graft union (if grafted onto herbaceous peony rootstock) 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots over time.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil sited where the shrub's permanent woody framework won't need to be moved again, since tree peonies resent transplanting once established. Unlike herbaceous peonies, Paeonia suffruticosa keeps a permanent woody structure through winter rather than dying back to the ground, slowly building a gnarled, long-lived shrub that can outlive the gardener who planted it; its huge, often ruffled or double blooms up to 8-10 inches across open in mid-to-late spring, roughly a week or two ahead of herbaceous peonies, in shades of white, pink, magenta, and deep maroon-purple depending on the selection. Give the plant full sun where summers are mild, but afternoon shade and reliable moisture where summers turn hot and humid, since tree peony foliage and flower quality both decline under intense heat stress. Avoid heavy spring or summer pruning, since flower buds form on old wood the prior season; remove only dead or damaged wood, and apply a light annual topdressing of compost rather than high-nitrogen fertilizer to avoid lush, disease-prone growth.

common_name: Rocket City Daylily (Tall Tetraploid Orange Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans or container divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Rocket City is a vigorous, heavy-blooming tetraploid that clumps up quickly and tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity without complaint.

directions: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and water deeply through the first season while the fans establish. Bred by Orville Fay and introduced in the early 1970s, Rocket City bears large, brilliant tangerine-orange, ruffled flowers with a green throat on tall, well-branched scapes that hold well above the foliage, and its tetraploid vigor gives it thick-textured petals and a heavier bud count than older diploid orange daylilies. Individual flowers have an extended bloom habit, staying open later into the evening than a typical single-day bloom, which stretches out the display during its main flowering flush in early summer. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the clump tidy and divide congested plantings every three to four years to maintain strong, floriferous growth.

common_name: Wizard Mix Coleus (Seed-Grown Multicolor Coleus Blend)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, surface-sowing since coleus seed needs light to germinate; transplant out after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: Surface-sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination, and transplant into partial shade to filtered sun once nights are reliably warm. Wizard Mix was one of the original All-America Selections-winning coleus lines bred to come true and uniform from seed rather than requiring cuttings, and the mix packet produces a full range of the series' signature colors on compact, well-branched plants, from deep maroon and rose to salmon, chartreuse, and bicolor combinations edged in green or cream. Pinch out the small blue flower spikes as they form to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage rather than seed production, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage bushy, well-filled plants. Wizard Mix tolerates more sun than older coleus strains but still colors up best and holds its leaves longest with some afternoon shade in hot Gulf South summers.

common_name: Washington Navel Orange (Classic Seedless Navel Orange)

planting.note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after the last frost in full sun with sharp drainage; Washington Navel is one of the least cold-hardy sweet oranges and needs a warm, sheltered site or container culture with winter protection outside zones 9b-10.

directions: Plant grafted trees in full sun in well-drained soil, keeping the graft union above the soil line, and water deeply and regularly while the tree establishes its root system. Washington Navel traces to a bud sport discovered in Bahia, Brazil in the early 1800s and became the foundation of the California citrus industry after Eliza Tibbets planted budwood from it in Riverside in 1873; it remains the standard by which other navel oranges are judged, prized for its large, easy-peeling, essentially seedless fruit with sweet, richly flavored flesh and the small secondary "navel" fruit embedded at the blossom end. Fruit ripens in winter and holds well on the tree for weeks without losing quality, but the tree itself is notably more cold-sensitive than many other sweet oranges, so gulf coast growers outside the mildest coastal pockets should plant it in a warm microclimate or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Fertilize lightly but regularly through the growing season and thin out crossing or dead wood in late winter to keep the canopy open.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Alley Cat colors best and resists leaf scorch with some afternoon shade, since its cream-and-white variegated leaves are more prone to sunburn than solid green redbud foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil sited with some relief from the hottest afternoon sun, which helps the variegated foliage hold its pattern instead of scorching at the leaf margins. Alley Cat is a variegated redbud selection bearing heart-shaped leaves heavily splashed and streaked in cream and white over green, giving the canopy a bright, almost frosted look through the growing season, and it produces the species' typical rosy-pink, pea-like flowers on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows as a smaller, slower tree than the straight species, staying more compact and tidy, which suits it well to a specimen spot in a shaded courtyard or woodland-edge planting where the bright foliage can be appreciated up close. Plant in well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites, and prune only to remove dead, crossing, or reverted all-green branches, since variegated shoots can occasionally revert and should be cut out to keep the tree true to type.
sources: J.C. Raulston Arboretum — Cercis Cultivar Trials

common_name: Gumpo White Azalea (Dwarf White Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Gumpo White is a low, dwarf Satsuki azalea that blooms noticeably later than most spring azaleas, extending the azalea season into early summer.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Gumpo White is a dwarf Satsuki azalea forming a low, dense, wide-spreading mound smothered in large, pure white, ruffled flowers that open several weeks later than most Southern Indica and Kurume azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, which makes it valuable for stretching the azalea display later into the season. Its low, compact habit and slow growth rate suit it especially well to foundation plantings, border edging, rock gardens, and container or bonsai culture, where its fine texture and heavy bloom show to best advantage. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends on this later-flowering type.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
